cls: Atypical tricyclic antidepressant - dopamine reuptake inhibitor (WITHDRAWN)
pharm: Tricyclic-structured antidepressant that, uniquely, acts mainly as a selective dopamine reuptake inhibitor and releaser, giving a stimulant-like profile
quick: Historical: 100-200 mg/day orally (e.g. 100 mg morning + 100 mg midday)
No reliable food guidance; rapidly absorbed
Hepatotoxic - contraindicated after prior amineptine hepatitis
Avoid - additive hepatic and CNS effects
Liver function tests; signs of dependence/abuse and severe acne
summary: Amineptine (Survector) was an atypical tricyclic antidepressant that, unusually for its class, acted mainly as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor and releaser, producing a stimulant-like, mood-elevating effect. It was introduced in France in 1978 for depression at doses of 100-200 mg/day, typically 100 mg in the morning and 100 mg at midday to avoid insomnia. It has been WITHDRAWN: France suspended marketing in 1999, and it is not available in the US (never FDA-approved), Germany and many other countries; the WHO recommended international control. The drug was abandoned because of a damaging triad of hepatotoxicity (cytolytic or cholestatic hepatitis), dependence/abuse potential driven by its dopaminergic action, and characteristic severe acne. This record is provided for historical reference only.
indications: Historical: treatment of depression (approved in France for severe/endogenous depression; now withdrawn)

dosage.d: 100-200 mg/day orally (one or two 100 mg tablets)
dosage.t: Dosed early in the day, e.g. 100 mg morning and 100 mg midday
dosage.n: Withdrawn - not for current clinical use

admin: Historically administered orally, dosed early in the day to avoid stimulant-induced insomnia
Not available for clinical use - withdrawn worldwide
If historical exposure is being assessed, monitor liver function
Assess for signs of dependence/misuse and characteristic severe acne
Do not co-administer with monoamine oxidase inhibitors
moa: Amineptine is a tricyclic-structured antidepressant that acts mainly as a selective/mixed dopamine reuptake inhibitor: it blocks the dopamine transporter, raising extracellular dopamine, and also promotes dopamine release (an indirect dopamine agonist). It has only a weak effect on noradrenaline reuptake and, distinctively for a TCA, interacts very weakly or not at all with serotonergic, adrenergic, histaminergic and muscarinic receptors. This dopaminergic action underlies both its antidepressant/stimulant effect and its abuse potential.

absolute: Pregnancy (first trimester) and breastfeeding; children under 15 years

preg: Amineptine was contraindicated in pregnancy (the first trimester explicitly cited) in its historical French labeling. It is not available for clinical use.
lact: Amineptine was contraindicated during breastfeeding per historical labeling.
renal: No specific renal dose-adjustment guidance is documented. Renal excretion occurs but no quantified adjustment exists in available sources.
hepatic: Hepatotoxicity is the defining safety problem. Amineptine causes cytolytic or cholestatic hepatitis, and prior amineptine-induced hepatitis is an explicit contraindication. It should be avoided in hepatic impairment; no graded hepatic dose-adjustment scheme exists.

moderate: Other dopaminergic, serotonergic or stimulant agents - caution (limited characterization)
interactions.food: No reliable food-effect guidance documented; the drug is rapidly absorbed (peak about 1 hour).
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive hepatotoxicity and central nervous system/stimulant effects (general caution; not directly sourced).
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor liver function tests given the hepatotoxicity risk.

common: Stimulant-type effects (short-lived euphoria, linked to misuse)
serious: Withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, insomnia, psychomotor agitation, bulimia)
emergency: Acute liver injury (jaundice, dark urine, right upper quadrant pain, malaise)

monitoring: Liver function tests (primary concern - cytolytic/cholestatic hepatitis)
Signs of dependence, misuse and withdrawal
counsel: This medicine has been withdrawn and is not recommended for use because of liver toxicity and abuse risk
Severe acne is a recognized effect, particularly with high-dose or long-term use
Seek urgent care for yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or right-sided abdominal pain
Do not use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding
pk: Antidepressant effect reported as early as day 7 historically
Plasma peak about 1 hour (parent); about 1.5 hours (main metabolite)
Short - parent about 0.8-1 hour; active metabolite about 1.5-2.5 hours
Short-acting with minimal accumulation; dosed early in the day
pearls: WITHDRAWN / NOT AVAILABLE - France 1999; not FDA-approved (US), banned in Germany and other countries; WHO recommended international control
The only TCA with meaningful dopamine-reuptake activity - hence its stimulant, euphoriant and abuse-prone profile
The triad that doomed it: hepatotoxicity, abuse/dependence, and characteristic severe (sometimes isotretinoin-resistant) acne
Severe acne, classically in women on high doses, is a near-pathognomonic clue to amineptine misuse
Contraindicated with MAOIs and after any prior amineptine-induced hepatitis
missed: Amineptine is withdrawn and not in clinical use, so missed-dose instructions are not applicable; given its short half-life, plasma levels fall quickly.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Manage supportively along general tricyclic/CNS-stimulant lines: benzodiazepines for seizures or agitation, fluids and vasopressors for hypotension, and consider activated charcoal for recent ingestion. Chronic overdose has been strongly associated with severe acne-like eruptions. Amineptine-specific protocols are sparse.
